title: The Sleeping Room
premise: Sebastian Sterling returns to Hollow Creek to bury his twin brother Julian, only to learn at the graveside that the body in the casket is not Julian at all — and that Julian vanished weeks ago while cataloguing the family estate. When an excavation crew unearths a door sealed from the inside beneath the old carriage house, Sebastian discovers Julian's notebooks describing a room that 'sleeps' the living, a debt incurred in 1974 when the Sterling patriarch stole a child's name to save his own skin. Guided by the notebooks and a woman named Ruth Ann, whose family the theft destroyed, Sebastian must return the stolen name to its rightful line before the harvest moon rises — or take Julian's place behind the sealed door. He succeeds, but only by surrendering his own claim to the Sterling inheritance, ending the family line and walking out of Hollow Creek as a stranger with no name of his own.
about_author: Ada Underhill is the pen name of a former county archivist who spent a decade cataloguing probate disputes and unsolved disappearances in rural Virginia. Her horror novels are known for their obsession with paperwork, inheritance law, and the quiet terror of official records that don't match the people they describe.

chapters.title: The Wrong Body
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. At the funeral home, Sebastian lifts the casket lid and finds a stranger wearing Julian's face — or close enough to unsettle everyone but him. The director blames grief; Sebastian begins photographing documents. The emotional beat is cold, controlled dread: the first crack in a world built on paperwork.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Missing Man
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. He returns to the decaying estate and finds Julian's meticulous notebooks, ending mid-sentence three weeks ago. The last entry mentions 'the room under the carriage house' and the year 1974. Beat: obsessive hope — documentation as prayer, and prayer as denial.

chapters.title: What the Crew Uncovered
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. The excavation crew, hired before Julian vanished, breaks through to a brick doorway sealed from the inside, its mortar fingered smooth from the far side. One worker refuses to return. Beat: the past stops being abstract and becomes load-bearing.

chapters.title: Ruth Ann of the Lower Field
chapters.summary: Ruth Ann's POV. A neighbor in her seventies recognizes Sebastian's face and calls him by his grandfather's name. She warns him off the carriage house and mentions a child taken in 1974 'to settle the count.' Beat: a witness who has been waiting fifty years to testify.

chapters.title: The 1974 File
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. In the county archive, Sebastian finds his grandfather's death record dated two years before the body was buried — and a birth certificate for a Sterling child no family member acknowledges. Beat: the thrill of the hunt curdling as the archive begins to feel watched.

chapters.title: Julian's Last Entry
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV, interleaved with Julian's notebook voice. Decoding Julian's shorthand, Sebastian learns his brother believed the sealed room 'sleeps' whoever the family owes, and that the debt has come due again. Beat: grief converting into mission.

chapters.title: The Count That Must Balance
chapters.summary: Ruth Ann's POV. She tells the story of 1974: the Sterlings' hired girl's son drowned in the cistern, and the family 'gave the room a name' so the county would look away. Beat: horror rooted in class injustice, not the supernatural alone.

chapters.title: Someone Answers the House Phone
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Late at night, the estate's dead landline rings; the voice on the line uses Julian's childhood nickname and asks Sebastian to 'come down and be counted.' Beat: the haunting becomes personal and intimate.

chapters.title: The Second Funeral
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. He holds a private, unofficial funeral for the stranger in the casket, and the town's quiet hostility surfaces — several families remember exactly whose boy was never buried in 1974. Beat: isolation; the town's complicity made visible.

chapters.title: Behind the Mortar
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. He breaches a corner of the sealed door and finds a room preserved like a diorama — a child's bed, school papers dated 1974, and Julian's coat folded neatly on the chair. Beat: hope and horror fused; Julian may be alive in there.

chapters.title: The Room Wakes
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. That night the house rearranges itself around him; doors he documented now open onto the sleeping room's corridor. His own notebook entries begin appearing in handwriting that is almost his. Beat: loss of control — the documenter becomes documented.

chapters.title: Ruth Ann's Bargain
chapters.summary: Ruth Ann's POV. She confesses she was the hired girl's sister, that she helped seal the door as a child, and that the room will accept restitution — a name returned to its rightful line — but only before the harvest moon. Beat: guilt, and the first real plan.

chapters.title: Probate of the Damned
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. He petitions to reopen the 1974 estate records and is stonewalled by families whose fortunes rest on the cover-up. A lawyer slips him the original file and warns him to leave town. Beat: justice outside the law becomes the only option.

chapters.title: The Name That Was Stolen
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. The file reveals the stolen name: Elias Boone, the drowned boy, erased so the Sterlings' heir could claim a birthright. Sebastian realizes the 'wrong body' in the casket was the room's down payment. Beat: the full shape of the inheritance crime.

chapters.title: Julian, Counted
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Through the breached corner, Sebastian speaks with Julian — alive, changed, insisting he is 'almost comfortable' and begging Sebastian not to undo it. Beat: the most painful temptation: peace offered at the price of forgetting.

chapters.title: What the Moon Requires
chapters.summary: Ruth Ann's POV. Two days before the harvest moon, Ruth Ann lays out the rite of return: the name must be given back publicly, in records and in blood, by a Sterling who chooses it. Beat: the cost is named; Sebastian begins deciding.

chapters.title: The House Objects
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. As he drafts the restitution deed, the estate turns violent — the sleeping room's corridor reaches into every room, and the house tries to finish Sebastian's documents in his hand. Beat: the antagonist stops being a mystery and becomes a will.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Eve
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. He burns his own claim to the Sterling inheritance, signs the name Elias Boone back into the county record, and walks to the carriage house with Ruth Ann as the moon rises fat and orange. Beat: resolve; the point of no return.

chapters.title: The Door, Unsealed
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV, climax. Inside the sleeping room, Sebastian offers the returned name and his own renunciation. The room demands a Sterling remain; Julian, half-dissolved into its peace, pushes Sebastian out and closes the door from the inside — this time by choice. Beat: sacrifice, reversal of the opening.

chapters.title: Elias Boone's Grave
chapters.summary: Ruth Ann's POV. They bury the stranger from the casket under the name Elias Boone, and the town's old families watch from their porches, saying nothing. Ruth Ann finally sleeps through the night. Beat: justice outside the law, imperfect but real.

chapters.title: A Man With No Inheritance
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. The county records Sebastian Sterling as deceased — the house took his name as payment. He packs his brother's notebooks and leaves Hollow Creek legally nobody, feeling lighter than he has in years. Beat: identity as burden shed; grief transmuted.

chapters.title: Documentation as Prayer
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV, coda. Months later, in a rented room far away, Sebastian writes the final entry: not to prove anything, but to remember. The last line — 'the count is balanced' — appears in handwriting that is almost his. Beat: quiet, unresolved grace; the story closes its own ledger.
